strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP problem: predicting answer failure before generation. A lightweight probe over frozen question representations offers a practical approach, and Table 2 documents substantial training savings while explicitly reporting representation-extraction costs.

The within-model results support the usefulness of question representations. The middle-layer, last-token variant achieves approximately 85–89% AUC on PopQA/Entity Questions and 69–71% on Natural Questions, generally matching or exceeding full fine-tuning and outperforming prompting and perplexity baselines.

The reported transfer gains are substantial across multiple model pairs. For example, LLaMA2-to-LLaMA3 transfer on PopQA improves from 0.443 to 0.842 AUC after adaptation. The additional Gemma experiment usefully examines transfer between different hidden dimensions.

The paper provides useful ablations on layers, token aggregation, entity representations, training size, kernels, and question-aligned batching. The matched-size dataset comparison and discussion of temporal and reasoning failures help characterize the method’s limitations.
weaknesses: The central inference in Section 5.1 is not justified. A pooled probe can recognize model-specific regions of representation space and learn different decision rules while matching separately trained probes. Thus, Figures 3–4 do not establish that the models share conditional distributions P(y|X) or lack concept shift. Equation 7 also asserts a strict advantage for aligned batches without conditions or proof; paired sampling does not universally improve distribution-distance estimation.

The unsupervised transfer evaluation needs a clearer, reproducible model-selection protocol. Appendix D does not adequately specify transfer checkpoint selection, while Figures 6 and 10 compare training trajectories and kernels using target-test AUC. This does not establish leakage, but the paper must explain how choices were made without target labels. Section 4.2 also includes validation examples in the stated training data despite validation-based tuning. Exact generation prompts, split identifiers, and seeds are missing.

Label validity is insufficiently established. Substring matching can miss correct alternative expressions and accept responses that mention an answer without asserting it correctly. The manual audit covers only 180 examples labeled factual, with 95% agreement; it does not validate the claimed correctness of all non-factual labels. Moreover, the explicit task definition combines refusals with incorrect answers and permits unrelated false claims, so the results support short-answer success prediction more directly than general factuality assessment.

Important controls are missing for interpreting the transfer contribution. A linear probe trained on the same correctness labels and a generic question-embedding classifier would help separate model-specific signals from question difficulty. Because training questions are paired across models, a particularly relevant baseline is training on target representations using source-model correctness labels. Evaluation on questions where source and target correctness disagree would further test the shared-pattern interpretation.

The paper reports no variability across seeds or confidence intervals, limiting confidence in small layer and baseline differences, particularly on the 1,244-question Natural Questions subset. AUC also does not establish calibrated factuality probabilities or useful abstention thresholds; the subjective study with 15 volunteers does not resolve this. The empirical contribution is promising, but the unsupported transfer interpretation and unresolved evaluation protocol prevent a clear Findings recommendation.
